title: Buying a Historic Home in San Antonio
description: Check local designation, exterior-work approvals and renovation records before building your historic-home improvement budget.

blocks.text: The porch, original windows and architectural details may be what draw you to an older San Antonio home. Your plans for the property deserve just as much attention before you buy. If replacing the windows, changing the exterior or adding space is essential to your decision, investigate the approval process before treating those changes as part of a settled renovation budget.
Quick answer

For a San Antonio property with a local historic zoning overlay, exterior alterations and repairs generally require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Office of Historic Preservation. The City's guidance includes side and rear areas that cannot readily be seen from the street. Confirm the property's status and the proposed work with OHP before scheduling a project.

links.label: City of San Antonio, Before Getting Started

blocks.text: Start with the address and your actual plans

Do not decide which rules apply from the home's age or appearance alone. Ask whether it is an individually designated landmark, part of a local historic district or subject to another design-review overlay. OHP's review responsibilities also include certain River Improvement Overlay and other designated areas. Ask City staff to identify the applicable process for the exact address.

links.label: City of San Antonio, About Design Review

blocks.text: Then write down the changes you would want to make. Separate the projects you consider essential from those you could postpone. A useful list might include replacement windows, a different roofing material, new siding, a porch alteration or a rear addition. Bring photographs and a description of the intended materials into the discussion. That makes the conversation more useful than asking generally whether the home can be remodeled.
Understand who reviews the work

A Certificate of Appropriateness, often shortened to COA, documents design-review approval. OHP says most items can be approved administratively by staff, while some proposals require a public hearing. Do not assume that every repair requires the same hearing process, or that approval is automatic.

links.label: City of San Antonio, About Design Review

blocks.text: The City's review structure also includes a technical advisory board that considers certain material-related requests, such as window and door replacement, roofing changes, and siding specifications. Ask which review route applies before assuming a contractor's proposed product is acceptable.

links.label: City of San Antonio, Boards and Commissions

blocks.text: This is a good point to compare two written scopes: the work you want and the work a contractor has priced. Ask the contractor to identify the exact materials and any assumptions about approval. If permission for a particular design has not been established, label that part of your budget as unresolved rather than treating the estimate as a ready-to-start plan.
Ask for records before relying on a renovation claim

Request copies of available COAs, approved drawings, invoices and related building-permit records for changes the seller describes. Compare the documents with the work visible at the property. If the paperwork describes one window type and the home appears to have another, ask for clarification rather than assuming either compliance or a violation.

Keep the design-review inquiry separate from the building-permit inquiry. San Antonio provides BuildSA resources and a legacy permit-search link for researching building records. A useful question for City staff is whether the particular project requires both a COA and separate permits.

links.label: City of San Antonio, BuildSA Online Services

blocks.text: Record unresolved questions with your agent before your contractual decision deadlines. Do not start work or order nonreturnable materials based only on a seller's recollection or a contractor's verbal assurance.
Clear up the paint question

San Antonio's current historic-district guidance says its Historic Design Guidelines do not limit paint-color selection. The review considers whether painting the underlying material is appropriate. For example, painting wood siding and painting historically unpainted brick raise different preservation issues. Permission to choose a color should not be confused with permission to paint every surface.

links.label: City of San Antonio, Historic Districts

blocks.text: If your plan changes the exterior finish, ask OHP about that precise scope before ordering materials. This is especially useful when the look you want depends on painting masonry or replacing original features.
Build an approval-aware timeline

The City directs COA applications through its online portal and recommends reviewing the process, design standards and application examples first. Have the responsible applicant confirm the required materials and review route. Avoid promising a construction start date before those steps are understood.

links.label: City of San Antonio, Submit an Application

blocks.text: Your buying checklist

items: Confirm the property's local designation and any other review overlay.
List the exterior changes that matter to your purchase decision.
Request approval and permit records for prior alterations.
Match contractor estimates to specific materials and an identified scope.
Ask which approval and permit steps remain unresolved.
Keep those questions visible before your contractual deadlines.

blocks.text: Questions buyers often ask
Does work in the backyard count?
It can. OHP's guidance includes exterior work in rear and side areas, even when it is not readily visible from the street. Confirm the specific project rather than relying on visibility alone.

links.label: City of San Antonio, Before Getting Started

blocks.text: Does every request go to a public hearing?
No. OHP says most items can receive administrative approval. The review route depends on the project.

links.label: City of San Antonio, About Design Review

blocks.text: Can I choose my paint color?
The City's current district guidance says the Historic Design Guidelines do not limit color selection. Whether a particular material should be painted is a separate review question.

links.label: City of San Antonio, Historic Districts

blocks.text: Planning a purchase

If you are considering a historic San Antonio property, contact Emily Russell to discuss how the home fits your plans and which property-specific questions should be organized before you move forward. City staff and qualified professionals should confirm approval requirements and technical feasibility.
This article provides general buyer education, not a property-specific approval, legal opinion or construction assessment.

title: How to Check San Antonio Permit History Before Buying a Home
description: Find San Antonio building permits, review inspection records and organize questions about a home’s renovations before buying.

blocks.text: A freshly remodeled kitchen can make a home feel move-in ready. Before you get too far into the buying process, add one more item to your research: the property’s permit history. For San Antonio properties, start with the City’s BuildSA resources and use the legacy portal for older records. Compare what you find with the improvements described by the seller. Permit research can help you ask more specific questions, but it cannot establish a home’s current condition.
Confirm the jurisdiction

San Antonio Development Services issues residential building permits for properties within city limits. First confirm that the address falls under the City’s jurisdiction. A home marketed as being in the San Antonio area may require research through another municipality or authority.
Search the appropriate records

The City directs people researching current projects to BuildSA. Its Legacy Permit Data Portal covers building permits issued from April 2003 through November 2020, plus a limited collection from 1998 through 2003. That older database includes only records that reached the issued stage and remain within applicable retention periods. An empty search should prompt a follow-up question rather than an immediate conclusion about the property.
Look beyond the permit number

The City’s inspection guide explains how to search BuildSA by address when you do not have a record number. Start with the street number and street name. After opening the relevant record, use Record Info, then Inspections, to review available inspection statuses and result comments. An account is not required to view inspection status. Ask Development Services if you are unsure which record matters.
Compare the records with the renovation story

Make a simple list of advertised improvements and the approximate dates the seller provides. Ask for available permits, invoices, warranties and related documentation. Some projects typically do not require permits. The City lists examples including cabinets, countertops, painting and certain flooring work. Historic, Neighborhood Conservation or Corridor District restrictions may still apply. Check the City’s exceptions list rather than assuming every cosmetic update should have a permit record.

links.label: Work that may not require a permit

blocks.text: Keep a short research log: the improvement, the record you found, what remains unclear and who can clarify it. Save record numbers so you can refer to the same project when speaking with the seller, your inspector or Development Services. A permit record is one part of your research, not a guarantee of workmanship or present-day safety. Continue with an independent inspection and appropriate specialist evaluation. Resolve questions early enough to inform your buying decisions, rather than leaving them until the final walkthrough. This article provides general educational information, not legal advice or a determination of a particular property’s compliance.
Three answers for readers
Where can I search San Antonio home permits?
Start with BuildSA for current records and the legacy portal for the older issued-permit collection. Confirm the jurisdiction first.
Do I need a BuildSA account to view inspection status?
No, according to the City’s inspection-status guide.
Does a missing permit record mean work was unpermitted?
Not necessarily. Coverage, retention, jurisdiction and permit exemptions can affect results. Ask Development Services about the project.

title: CPS Energy Move-in Checklist for San Antonio Homebuyers
description: Confirm electric and gas service, account dates, permanent service and billing questions before your San Antonio move.

blocks.text: Before moving into a San Antonio-area home, confirm the utility provider for the address, arrange your service dates, and ask whether permanent electric and gas service is ready. For an existing home, that usually means coordinating an account start or transfer. For new construction, ask the builder about the remaining utility work before planning around a move-in date.
Keep these questions beside your closing checklist so utility arrangements do not become a last-minute surprise.
1 Verify the address and the services you need

Start with the complete street address, including any unit number. CPS Energy publishes separate electric-service and gas-availability maps. Confirm service directly for the property rather than relying on its postal city or a nearby home's provider.

Ask which appliances use gas and which use electricity. Record the water heater, heating system, range and dryer connections. Those details help you ask useful questions about service needs and avoid choosing replacement appliances before you understand the house.
2 Put the service request on your calendar

CPS Energy's online account agreement requires two business days' notice for new accounts and transfers at existing residences. Requests can be processed up to 30 days ahead, and starts and transfers cannot be scheduled on weekends or CPS Energy holidays.

Coordinate your requested date with your possession arrangements, then retain the confirmation. If closing moves, review the utility dates promptly. The residential service page links to starting service and directs transfers through Manage My Account.
3 For a new build ask about permanent service

For homes using an existing underground distribution system, CPS Energy's construction process includes separate temporary and permanent service steps. Activation also depends on applicable inspection requirements. A visible meter alone does not establish that service is active: the utility explains that an electric meter can remain locked while required inspection information is outstanding.
Ask the builder for a clear update:

items: Is permanent electric service active at this home?
If gas is included, is that service active too?
What work or approvals remain, and who is handling each item?
What date has the utility actually confirmed?

blocks.text: Use the answers when discussing the final walkthrough and moving schedule. Do not treat the ordinary account-start notice period as a completion promise for unfinished construction.
4 Allow for deposits and read the whole bill

A deposit may be required when establishing service. CPS Energy says it will contact customers if additional information or deposit details are needed. Ask about the requirements for your own account instead of assuming a seller's or friend's experience will apply.

When comparing ownership costs, review more than the energy-use line. CPS Energy's bill guide explains base charges, fuel adjustments and regulatory adjustments. Some City of San Antonio services, including garbage collection, can also appear on the bill. Separate those items when building your monthly budget.
5 Compare a full year when records are available

Ask the seller for 12 months of bills, if available, with account numbers and payment details removed. Compare usage, billing days and seasonal changes as well as the total charged. Note differences between the seller's household and yours, such as occupancy, thermostat habits or vehicle charging. Past bills provide context, not a promise about your future costs.
After your account is active, Manage My Account provides access to bills, energy usage and My Energy Portal. Use your own records to refine the budget as you settle in.
6 Keep one utility record for your move

Create a simple list with each provider, requested start date, confirmation reference and unresolved question. Keep the seller's stop date and your start date coordinated through the appropriate people. Water, internet and any other services need their own arrangements.

Save the first bill with your closing paperwork. If the address, dates or charges look unfamiliar, ask the provider to explain them. This small record makes it easier to follow up without searching through moving boxes and old messages.
Planning a San Antonio-area home purchase? Contact Emily Russell at (210) 912-0806 to discuss your home search and move timeline. Bring your utility questions into the conversation before closing.
General educational information, Confirm service availability, account requirements and property-specific timing directly with the utility and builder.
Quick answers
How early should I request CPS Energy service?
For an existing residence, CPS Energy requires two business days' notice and accepts requests up to 30 days ahead. Weekend and holiday restrictions apply.
Does a meter mean power is on in a new home?
No. CPS Energy explains that an electric meter can remain locked pending required inspections. Ask the builder to confirm active permanent service.
Will my bill match the previous bill?
Do not assume so. Compare the usage history, then allow for your household's habits and the charges applicable to your account.

title: San Antonio New Construction Property Tax Estimates
description: Understand January 1 valuations, unfinished construction and homestead exemptions when comparing new-home tax estimates.

blocks.text: When comparing new homes, a low property-tax estimate deserves a closer look. The number may reflect the lot before construction or the house while it was unfinished. For a home in Bexar County, checking the January 1 valuation date and the land-and-improvement breakdown can make the difference between a useful budget and a misleading comparison.
Here is how to read the estimate before choosing your finishes, upgrades, or floor plan.
Find out what existed on January 1

Bexar Central Appraisal District values property according to its status on January 1. If a house was unfinished that day, BCAD says it is valued at a partial percentage reflecting its completion level. Improvements that did not exist on January 1 are not included for that year. BCAD’s residential-property guidance explains this timing.

The budgeting implication: a bill based on an empty lot or partially completed house may understate the cost after the finished home enters the valuation. Completion later in the year does not make the earlier bill a reliable full-year forecast. Do not assume every new home is initially taxed only on its land; verify the actual property record.
Compare land and improvement values

Open the property’s BCAD record and check the tax year first. The Values & Roll History section may show land value, improvement value, market value, appraised value, taxable value, and prior-year information. The Improvements section can show the building’s size, year built, construction characteristics, and condition. Available details vary by property and year. BCAD’s property-search guide explains the fields.

Compare the land and improvement amounts with the estimate you were given. Ask whether the house is represented as completed construction, partial construction, or absent from that year’s valuation. A small improvement value is a reason to ask questions; it does not establish an error by itself.
Use every applicable taxing unit

The appraisal district determines values and exemptions; local taxing units adopt rates. The tax office applies those rates to certified values after applicable exemptions. Bexar County describes the calculation process here.

links.label: Source  Bexar County describes the calculation process here.

blocks.text: A county rate alone does not represent the entire bill. Check the property’s actual jurisdictions, then use the appropriate year’s rates. Bexar County’s 2026 rate-and-exemption table lists rates per $100 of taxable value.

For a simplified example, $260,000 of taxable value at $1.00 per $100 produces $2,600 for one taxing unit. Calculate each applicable unit separately because exemptions may differ, then add the results. This example is not a quoted local rate or a property-specific estimate.
Budget for the completed home
Verify the homestead assumptions

The Texas Comptroller currently lists a $140,000 general residence-homestead exemption for school-district taxes. Other taxing units can have different exemptions, so the same deduction should not automatically be applied throughout the bill.

Eligibility generally requires an ownership interest and use of the home as the owner’s principal residence. Applicants must state that they do not claim another residence-homestead exemption inside or outside Texas.

A buyer acquiring a home after January 1 may qualify for the applicable portion of that year if the previous owner did not receive the same exemption that year. Confirm eligibility and timing with BCAD before budgeting for savings. Texas Comptroller exemption guidance.
Know how new improvements affect the 10 percent limit

The homestead appraisal limitation generally begins January 1 of the tax year after the owner qualifies for the exemption. The calculation limits appraised value to the lower of market value or the prior year’s appraised value plus 10%, plus the market value of qualifying new improvements.

New improvements are added separately in that formula. The limitation concerns appraised value; it does not guarantee that the total tax bill can increase by no more than 10%. Texas Comptroller valuation guidance.
Ask for two clearly labeled scenarios

Before closing, request a current-year estimate and a future full-year estimate based on the completed home. Ask each preparer to identify the land and improvement values, tax year, jurisdictions, rates, and exemptions used.
Future values and rates remain uncertain. Keeping those assumptions visible makes it easier to compare homes and reserve room in the budget for the property you will actually own.
Questions to ask before closing

items: Which tax year and property value support this estimate?
Does the estimate include the completed home?
Which taxing units and exemptions were included?
What would the estimate be without exemptions not yet confirmed?
How could changing taxes affect the escrow payment?

blocks.text: Keep the answers with your loan estimate and closing records so you can compare the assumptions with later notices.
Frequently asked questions
How much is the Bexar County homestead exemption in 2026?
The mandatory school-district exemption is $140,000 for qualifying residence homesteads. Other taxing units’ exemptions differ.
Can I qualify if I buy after January 1?
Possibly. BCAD says buyers may qualify for the remainder of the year if the previous owner was not already claiming the exemption. Confirm eligibility with BCAD.
Can my payment change with a fixed-rate mortgage?
Yes. Taxes and homeowners insurance can change, affecting the escrow portion and total monthly payment even when the interest rate is fixed.
General educational information. This article is not individualized tax or legal advice. Consult the appraisal district, tax office, or a qualified adviser about a specific property.

title: San Antonio New-Build Inspections: City vs. Home Inspector
description: Learn how City inspections and a buyer’s home inspection differ, what to ask and which records to review before closing.

blocks.text: A newly built home comes with plenty of paperwork. Before closing, ask two separate questions: what inspections were completed through the permitting authority, and what will your own inspector examine? Understanding both can help you organize the information you need before making a purchase decision.

For San Antonio buyers, start with the home's actual jurisdiction. The City’s residential permitting guidance applies to homes located within the City. Confirm which authority handles the specific property before relying on a permit search.
What the City reviews

San Antonio Development Services reviews construction plans and conducts inspections tied to building permits. Its work addresses compliance with the City’s adopted building codes and development requirements. The department’s inspection teams cover building, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work.

Ask the builder for the permit number, the responsible permitting authority and the status of required inspections. The City provides online services for checking permit status. If a record is unclear, ask Development Services to explain what it shows and whether any required steps remain. Keep the response with your purchase documents.
What your home inspector examines

A Texas real estate inspection evaluates the home’s general condition when the inspection takes place. TREC describes it as a limited visual review and basic performance evaluation of accessible systems and components. The standards set minimum requirements for inspections of substantially completed one-to-four-family homes.

That scope has limits. The standard inspection report explains that an inspection may not reveal every deficiency and does not verify building-code compliance. Hidden conditions and inaccessible areas can remain outside what the inspector can evaluate. Read the limitations and ask which parts of the home were accessible on the inspection date.
Ask about timing before scheduling

Discuss inspection access and timing with your builder, agent and inspector early. Ask whether the home will be substantially complete, which utilities will be operating and how much time you will have to review findings before your contractual deadlines.

If you want an inspection during construction, ask the inspector to explain that service separately. TREC’s rules recognize exceptions to the standard reporting requirements for buildings that are not substantially complete and certain builder quality-control inspections. Get the scope, deliverable and fee in writing so you understand exactly what you are purchasing.
Choose an inspector and read the whole report

TREC’s consumer guidance points buyers to its License Holder Search, where you can review licensing information, disciplinary history and education. Ask prospective inspectors about their experience with the type of home you are buying, what the quoted service includes and whether additional evaluations may be needed.

Once the report arrives, read the complete document. Ask the inspector to explain unfamiliar findings and any recommendations for another professional’s evaluation. TREC encourages buyers to address follow-up evaluations before applicable contractual deadlines, including an option period when one applies.

A deficiency recorded in the inspection report does not itself require the builder or seller to make a repair. Any repair request, agreement or contractual question needs its own review. The report also does not automatically include a return visit to verify repairs, so ask about that service if you need it.
Keep one clear record

Save the permit information, inspection report, questions, written responses and any repair agreements together. A simple folder works. Label documents by date and keep unresolved items visible so they are easier to discuss before closing.
Buying new construction around San Antonio? Bring your inspection questions into the conversation early, alongside the price, timeline and contract terms.
General educational information, Confirm property-specific requirements with the relevant permitting authority and qualified professionals.
Quick answers
Does a City inspection replace a buyer’s home inspection?
They address different scopes. City inspections address permitted construction and code requirements; a buyer’s inspection evaluates accessible systems and the home’s general condition. City
Does a home inspection guarantee a defect-free new home?
No. TREC’s standard report explains that the inspection is limited and may not uncover every deficiency.
Where can I check a Texas home inspector’s credentials?
Use TREC’s License Holder Search. Its consumer guide also explains how to review disciplinary history and education.

title: Buying a San Antonio Home: Water, Trees and Drainage
description: Review water use, irrigation, drainage, foundation findings and tree care before buying a San Antonio home.

blocks.text: A beautiful kitchen is easy to notice during a home tour. Water use, drainage and tree care deserve time on your checklist, too. For a San Antonio buyer, the useful questions are practical: Who provides the water? What has the property used? Where does runoff go? What needs a closer inspection?
Start gathering answers before your inspection deadline. Bring the address, utility bills and any repair records into the conversation with your agent, inspector and appropriate specialists.
1 Check the water rules for this address

Check the current watering stage and permitted irrigation hours directly with your water provider. SAWS restrictions can change, and assigned watering days depend on the street address. Confirm the current schedule before programming the controller.

Ask the seller to show you the irrigation controller and explain its schedule. Verify the actual water provider before applying SAWS guidance to a property elsewhere in the metro area. Recheck current restrictions when you move in.
2 Request bills and find the shutoff

Ask for a year of water bills, if available, and compare gallons used as well as dollars charged. A household’s habits will differ from yours, but a large seasonal jump is worth discussing. Ask whether the property has irrigation, a pool or any known leaks.

SAWS maintains the water line from the main to the meter. Repairs from the meter toward the home are the owner’s responsibility. Have the seller or a qualified professional identify the customer shutoff, and ask your inspector which visible plumbing components and leak indicators will be evaluated.
3 Read the foundation and drainage findings together

During your inspection, pay attention to the written foundation opinion and the grading-and-drainage section. Texas inspection standards address visible foundation-performance indicators and require reporting deficient drainage around the foundation, grade levels, gutters and downspouts.

Ask about past foundation work, drainage changes and related documents. A standard inspection has limits: it is a visual survey and basic performance evaluation, and it does not require a sewer-camera inspection or foundation-elevation measurements. If concerns remain, consider a qualified structural engineer or other relevant specialist before your decision deadline. Avoid guessing at repairs from a crack photograph alone.
4 Give mature trees their own review

Ask about the trees’ watering history, previous pruning and any recent decline. Texas A&M Forest Service advises checking soil moisture and following the local water provider’s restrictions during drought. Its guidance also recommends avoiding digging beneath the canopy and applying high-salt, quick-release fertilizers during severe drought.

If a tree’s condition or location raises questions, arrange an assessment with a certified arborist. Keep tree-care recommendations and foundation recommendations specific to the property. A general watering tip should not become a diagnosis of structural damage or an automatic reason to remove a tree.

links.label: Texas A&M Forest Service drought guidance

blocks.text: 5. Include changing utility costs

There is a timely budgeting detail for fall buyers. SAWS says winter water use helps determine sewer charges for the following year. Its October reminder places the averaging season roughly between mid-November and mid-March, with the exact dates depending on the billing cycle. Ask SAWS how a new account’s sewer average will be established.

Also allow for changing rates: SAWS announced that an approved adjustment beginning January 1, 2027, would increase the average monthly residential bill by less than $4. Your bill will depend on your account and usage. Review the irrigation schedule as temperatures cool rather than automatically keeping summer settings.
Build a useful ownership file

Keep the inspection report, specialist findings, repair records, utility information and irrigation instructions together. Use unresolved questions to guide your next conversation before closing. The goal is a clearer picture of the home’s condition, upkeep and recurring costs, so you can choose a property with fewer unanswered questions.

title: San Antonio Home Insurance Checklist Before Closing
description: Compare roof coverage, dollar deductibles, claim records and policy start dates when choosing homeowners insurance.

blocks.text: Before closing on a San Antonio home, get an insurance quote for the specific address, check how the roof would be covered, convert percentage deductibles to dollars, and confirm the policy's start date with your insurance professional and lender. The annual premium is only one part of the decision.

A home can fit your purchase-price budget while carrying an insurance arrangement that leaves you with a large out-of-pocket repair bill. Asking these questions early gives you time to compare the actual terms and resolve property-specific issues before the closing appointment.
Start with the house you are actually buying

Request quotes using the correct address and accurate information about the property. Keep a copy of the details supplied, including the roof's age if it can be documented. If an answer is unknown, flag it for the agent instead of guessing. Ask what additional information or inspection the insurer needs before coverage can begin.

For a useful comparison, ask each insurance professional to explain the proposed limits, deductibles, coverage type, optional endorsements and exclusions. A lower premium can come with different protection. Texas Department of Insurance's shopping checklist specifically encourages buyers to compare rebuilding coverage, personal property, other structures, living expenses and liability.

Keep the written quote and its date. Ask how long it remains valid and whether the price depends on bundling, a particular payment method, or information still awaiting verification. These answers belong beside the premium when you compare options.
Separate rebuilding coverage from the sale price

Ask the insurance professional how the dwelling coverage amount was calculated. The amount needed to rebuild the house is a different question from what you are paying for the property. Do not substitute the purchase price or a property-tax value without asking how the insurer estimates reconstruction costs.

Also review the limits for belongings, detached structures and additional living expenses if a covered loss makes the home unlivable. TDI's home insurance guide explains that coverage categories have their own limits and that flood damage is generally outside a standard home policy. Ask about exclusions and any separate coverage relevant to the address.
Read the roof settlement terms
Ask a direct question: If a covered storm damages this roof, will the policy settle the loss using replacement cost, actual cash value, or another stated schedule?

Replacement-cost coverage generally uses current repair or replacement costs, subject to the policy. Actual-cash-value coverage subtracts depreciation for age or condition. TDI warns that some insurers change roof coverage as a roof gets older, and a roof in poor condition may not be covered. Ask for the roof terms and relevant endorsements in writing.

For illustration, imagine the same covered roof repair under two policies. The premium may look attractive under the policy that deducts depreciation, but more of the repair cost could fall to the homeowner. Ask the agent to walk through a dollar example using the proposed deductible and settlement terms. TDI's comparison shows why roof age can affect actual-cash-value payments.
Turn every percentage deductible into dollars

A percentage sounds small until it is converted to money. Suppose a hypothetical policy applies a 2% wind-and-hail deductible to $350,000 of dwelling coverage. The deductible would be $7,000. That example is arithmetic, not an estimate of the right coverage or deductible for your house.

Ask which insured amount the percentage uses, whether wind and hail have a separate deductible, and what applies to other covered losses. TDI explains that home-insurance deductibles generally apply to each claim rather than once per year.

Write the dollar amount beside each quote and consider how you would cover it. Also ask what other deductions or limits could affect payment. A deductible alone does not describe the entire amount you might need to pay after a loss.
Ask the seller about claims and repair records

TDI says a buyer can ask the current owner to show a Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange, or CLUE, report for the property. It generally reflects claims reported over the previous seven years. Insurers may consider that history when deciding whether to offer coverage and what to charge.

If a reported claim raises a question, ask for the related repair records and discuss the issue with the appropriate professional. Compare those records with the seller's disclosures and inspection findings. A claim entry alone does not explain the quality of a repair; an absence of listed claims is not a substitute for inspecting the home.
Keep this information private. The purpose is to understand the transaction and proposed coverage, not to publish the seller's insurance history in a neighborhood group or marketing post.
Reconcile the policy with closing

Your lender will generally require homeowners insurance for a mortgaged property. Confirm the required coverage, proof of insurance and effective date with both the lender and insurance professional. Ask who is responsible for sending each document.

Review the insurance amounts and escrow information on your Closing Disclosure. CFPB's explainer shows where to check which expenses are included in escrow and encourages borrowers to question unexpected differences. Match the selected policy's premium to the closing paperwork and clarify how it will be paid.

For the ongoing budget, keep the premium and possible deductible in separate lines. The first is a recurring cost; the second is an exposure you may face when making a covered claim. The site's tax and escrow checklist explains why the monthly mortgage payment can later change.
Make a simple record after moving in

Create a home inventory as you unpack. Photographs or video, purchase records and serial numbers can help document belongings. TDI recommends keeping the inventory somewhere safe away from the home or in online storage, and updating it as possessions change.

Before you close, aim to answer five questions: What is covered? How is the roof valued? What would each deductible cost in dollars? What property information remains unresolved? When does the policy start? Save the written answers with the policy and closing records so they are easy to find later.

General educational information. Insurance availability, terms and claim payments depend on the insurer, policy, property and circumstances. Ask a licensed insurance professional for coverage advice and your transaction professionals about purchase-specific deadlines.

title: San Antonio Title Commitment, Survey and Easement Checklist
description: Review title commitments, survey details and easements together before relying on plans for your new property.

blocks.text: General educational information. Ask a Texas real-estate attorney about legal rights, contract deadlines, and property-specific restrictions; ask the title company and surveyor about their respective documents.

Before closing on a San Antonio home, put three things side by side: the title commitment, the property survey, and the documents behind any listed exceptions. Together, they help you ask better questions about the land being transferred, rights held by others, and the coverage the title insurer is offering.

A spacious backyard can make it easy to picture a future shed, pool, or garden. Before building those plans into your purchase decision, make room for a paperwork review. The useful question is specific: do the documents support the way you want to use this particular property?
1 Ask for the complete document set

Start a folder containing the purchase contract, title commitment, survey, and copies of the recorded documents referenced in the commitment. Keep later revisions in date order so you know which version everyone is discussing.

The Texas Department of Insurance explains that a commitment comes before closing and describes the conditions under which a company is willing to issue title insurance. It does not guarantee that the property has no existing or future title problems. An owner's policy protects the owner under its terms; a lender's policy protects the lender. Ask which policies are proposed and what each covers.

links.label: Texas Department of Insurance: title insurance FAQ

blocks.text: If an attachment is missing or unreadable, request a legible copy promptly. A reference number alone is difficult to evaluate when you are trying to understand an actual driveway, fence, or utility corridor.
2 Give each part of the commitment a job
Texas's standard commitment form provides a useful reading order:

items: Schedule A: Check the proposed insured, policy amount, ownership information, and legal description.
Schedule B: Identify exceptions, meaning matters excluded from the proposed coverage.
Schedule C: Identify requirements that must be addressed for the insurer to provide the contemplated coverage.

blocks.text: The form also explains that policy exclusions and conditions affect coverage. Reading only the exception list will not answer every insurance question. Request the proposed policy form and ask the title company to explain unfamiliar wording.

links.label: TDI: Commitment for Title Insurance, Form T-7

blocks.text: Make a short question list using the schedule and item number. “What does Schedule B, item 12 mean for the side driveway?” is easier to investigate than “Is the title okay?” Keep the answer with the document it explains.
3 Check what the survey actually represents

Ask who prepared the survey, when it was prepared, and whether it reflects changes made since then. Compare it with what you saw during the property visit. Note a newer patio, moved fence, detached structure, or changed driveway, and ask the surveyor and title company whether the drawing needs updating.

An existing survey may be acceptable for title-insurance purposes, but acceptance is not automatic. TDI's rules allow an insurer to accept an existing survey with the required supporting affidavit or declaration. The rules also allow an unsworn T-47.1 declaration in place of a T-47 affidavit. Ask what this transaction requires rather than assuming an old drawing will be sufficient.

Also ask whether the proposed policy's area-and-boundary exception will be amended, what that costs, and what specific exceptions would remain. Having a survey does not by itself settle the scope of the insurance coverage.
4 Turn an easement reference into practical questions

An easement gives someone a right to use another person's property for a particular purpose. Common examples include utility access, a public sidewalk, or a private access road. Written easements are often recorded with the county, but some easements can arise without a written agreement.
For each relevant easement, ask:

items: Where is it, and can it be located on the survey?
Who has the right to use it, and for what purpose?
What does the document say about access and maintenance?
Could it affect a planned fence, pool, shed, or other improvement?

blocks.text: As a hypothetical example, a buyer might see enough lawn for a detached workshop but discover an easement through the intended location. The next step is to understand the document and seek property-specific advice before spending money on plans. Avoid assuming either that every easement prevents construction or that an existing structure proves permission.
5 Use Bexar County records as a cross-check

For a property in Bexar County, the County Clerk's Official Records Search includes land records and plats. The county describes it as a free online resource for searching and viewing documents, with uncertified copies available to print. Start from the county's own page and select the relevant record category.

Use the recording references supplied by the title company to locate the right documents. Confirm that the legal description and recording details match the property under discussion. If the home is outside Bexar County, use the clerk serving that property's county.
A personal records search is useful preparation, but the County Clerk does not guarantee clear title. Take unresolved questions to the title company or an attorney.

links.label: Bexar County: real property and land records

blocks.text: 6 Put document review on the contract calendar

Do not leave this folder until the closing appointment. TREC's current resale form separates title-policy, survey, and objection provisions in Paragraph 6. Its objection process has deadlines, and failing to object within the allowed time can waive certain rights. The actual signed contract controls, including its completed blanks and any amendments.

TREC currently lists resale form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026. That form is not intended for builder sales of new homes, condominium transactions, or farm-and-ranch properties. Ask the professional reviewing your transaction which provisions apply.

links.label: TREC: current One to Four Family Residential Contract

blocks.text: Keep a dated log of when the commitment, exception documents, survey, and revisions arrive. Ask your attorney to confirm the relevant review and notice dates. Do not assume the inspection or option-period calendar answers every title question.
Your pre-closing question list
Before the final document review, aim to have clear answers to five questions:

items: 1. Does the legal description match the property I intend to buy?
2. Which survey is being used, and have changes been addressed?
3. Which easements or other exceptions affect my intended use?
4. What requirements remain unresolved, and who is handling each one?
5. What coverage will the final owner's policy provide?

blocks.text: Save the final policy and supporting records after closing. A well-organized folder gives you a better starting point when a future project raises questions about the land you own.

title: Buying a San Antonio Home With Solar Panels
description: Check ownership, leases, CPS Energy records, production, warranties and current incentive rules before closing.

blocks.text: Buying a San Antonio home with solar panels? Start by confirming who owns the equipment, what payments or contracts remain, and what the system actually produces. Then review the roof, warranties, utility records and transfer requirements before your purchase deadlines. Panels on the roof are only one part of the picture.
This checklist focuses on homes with an existing rooftop system. Utility-specific guidance below applies to CPS Energy customers; confirm the provider for the property you are considering.
Find out who owns the equipment

Ask the seller for the original purchase agreement and any loan, lease, power-purchase or service agreements connected to the system. The Department of Energy recommends identifying the ownership arrangement because a third-party-owned system may involve additional contract-transfer steps.

links.label: DOE guide to buying a home with solar panels

blocks.text: Get written answers to three questions:

items: Which equipment would be included in the home sale?
Would any solar payment continue after closing?
Who must approve a payoff, transfer or assumption?

blocks.text: Have your lender, title company and, where needed, attorney review the relevant documents. Ask them to identify any financing or title issues that need resolution. A listing's description of the panels as “owned” does not answer every question about an outstanding loan.
Review any lease before agreeing to take it over

Texas has a specific TREC Addendum Regarding Fixture Leases, Form 52-1, that expressly includes solar panels. The form addresses which leases the buyer will assume, assignment costs, delivery of lease documents and other terms. It also tells the parties to consult the lessor and their attorneys about assignment, assumption or termination.

Ask your real-estate team which documents apply to your transaction. Review payment increases, remaining term, transfer conditions and any end-of-term obligations in the actual solar agreement. Put relevant dates on your purchase calendar. Do not assume that requesting more information changes a contract deadline.
Ask for installation and utility approval records

For a CPS Energy property, request the interconnection paperwork, applicable permits and inspection records, and the Permission to Operate email or equivalent utility confirmation for the installation.

CPS Energy's published residential installation process distinguishes approval to install from final commissioning and activation. It describes a Permission to Operate email after successful commissioning. A sales proposal or equipment invoice alone does not establish that those final steps occurred.

Ask CPS Energy what, if anything, a change of property owner requires for this particular system and account. Keep that answer with your closing checklist rather than assuming that starting electric service completes every solar-related step.
Compare electricity bills with solar payments

Request a full year of available electric bills and system-production records. Read the dates together so you can compare the same periods. If records are incomplete, make that gap part of your review.

CPS Energy's solar billing guide distinguishes energy delivered by the utility, surplus energy sent back to the grid and net billed consumption. The examples also show a service-availability charge and, when applicable, an excess-generation credit. The sample dollar amounts illustrate billing; they are not a current quote for your home.

Build your estimate from the electric bill plus any solar obligation you would assume, maintenance expectations and insurance costs. Ask the utility to explain current rates and credits. Your household's usage can differ from the seller's, so last year's bills should inform your questions rather than become a savings guarantee.
Review the roof and the system together
Find out when the roof and solar equipment were installed. DOE recommends considering the system's age alongside the roof's age.

Ask your inspector what the inspection will cover and whether a solar specialist or roofer should evaluate anything further. Request equipment model numbers, maintenance records and the actual manufacturer and installer warranties.
Useful follow-up questions include:

items: What remains covered, and can that coverage transfer to the buyer?
Are there transfer fees, registration steps or deadlines?
Who handles roof leaks or equipment problems?
What would panel removal and reinstallation involve if roof work becomes necessary?

blocks.text: Also ask your insurance provider how the system would be covered under your proposed policy. Get the answer for this equipment and ownership arrangement.
Confirm what works during an outage

Solar panels alone do not establish that a home has backup power. DOE explains that many grid-connected residential systems lose power when the grid goes down. Backup capability depends on the installed equipment and configuration.

If backup power is part of the property's appeal, ask a qualified solar professional to explain which circuits are supported, the usable storage capacity and the system's operating limits. Request the manuals and a safe orientation. Do not test or alter electrical equipment yourself.
Check incentive claims against current rules
CPS Energy's residential rooftop-solar page currently says it does not offer rebates for residential solar installations. Older rebate references should not be used to build a new purchase budget.

Federal rules also changed. The IRS says the Residential Clean Energy Credit is unavailable for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, and that previously owned clean-energy equipment is ineligible. Its updated FAQ confirms that completing installation after that date does not qualify merely because payment occurred earlier. Do not assume buying a home with existing panels creates a new 30% federal credit. Ask a qualified tax professional about your circumstances.
Common buyer questions
Do solar panels automatically become mine when I buy the house?

Confirm ownership and the sale documents. Third-party ownership, leases and financing can require additional review or transfer steps. Obtain written answers from the parties responsible before relying on a listing description.
Will solar panels eliminate my CPS Energy bill?

Do not assume they will. CPS Energy's billing examples include service charges, net billed electricity and possible excess-generation credits. Your result depends on the applicable billing rules and the home's production and consumption.
Does a solar lease need its own review?

Yes. Read the agreement and transfer requirements with your real-estate team. TREC's fixture-lease addendum specifically includes solar panels, but the signed documents determine the transaction's obligations and deadlines.
Will the panels power the house during an outage?
That depends on the system. Have a qualified professional verify the backup equipment, configuration and supported loads. The presence of rooftop panels by itself is insufficient.
Keep one packet for your purchase review

Before your decision deadlines, gather the ownership and financing documents, lease terms if applicable, utility approval records, recent bills, production history, warranties and inspection findings. Record each open question, who can answer it and when the answer is needed. Bring that packet to your real-estate team so unresolved solar details are visible while you still have time to address them.

General educational information. Contract, utility, insurance and tax treatment depend on the property and circumstances. Consult the appropriate licensed professionals for transaction-specific advice.

title: San Antonio Water Service and Sewer Billing Checklist
description: Confirm providers, account setup, deposits, winter averaging and meter checks before moving into a San Antonio home.

blocks.text: Before buying a San Antonio home, confirm who supplies its water, who bills for sewer service, and how to start an account for your move-in date. Then check deposits and the billing rules that will apply to you. A few address-specific questions can make your first utility bill easier to plan for.
Confirm water and sewer service separately

Start with the exact property address, including a unit number if there is one. Ask the seller which companies currently send the water and wastewater bills, then confirm that information directly with the providers.

San Antonio Water System publishes separate water and sewer service-area maps. SAWS explains that the two areas differ and that it also supplies wholesale water to smaller utilities. A San Antonio mailing address alone is not enough to settle who will open your account or send your bill.

Ask whether the home has its own meter, shares service through a building, or uses a different arrangement. For a newly built home, confirm with the builder and utility whether the permanent meter and service are ready. Save the provider’s answer with your moving checklist.
Choose the right account setup route

If you are new to SAWS, use the Start Service option on its official website. If you already have a SAWS account and are moving, sign in to My Account to stop or transfer service. SAWS also lists 210-704-7297 for assistance.

The published new-service checklist includes the property address, a valid driver’s license or Texas ID, a contact phone number, a mailing address and your date of birth. Provide those details directly to the utility through its official process.

Coordinate your requested start date with the seller’s planned stop date and the date you will take possession. Ask SAWS to confirm availability, any extra documentation and the effective date in writing. Keep the confirmation; do not assume that closing on the property has completed this step.
Allow for the initial deposit

SAWS lists a standard residential deposit of $100 for combined water and sewer service in its 2026 fee schedule. Water-only and sewer-only deposits differ, and lower deposits are listed for Uplift Assistance Program customers. Ask which deposit and any additional service fees apply to your account. These initial charges are separate from estimating your regular monthly use.
Ask how the first sewer bills will be calculated

SAWS uses winter water consumption to estimate residential sewer use. Its winter-averaging guidance describes three consecutive billing periods between mid-November and mid-March. The dates depend on the customer’s billing cycle, and SAWS updates the schedule each year.

A new customer may not yet have a winter usage record. The residential rate page says customers without a winter record or an interim average are billed using an assumed 5,985 gallons of monthly sewer use. Ask which basis will apply when your account starts and when your own average can be established.

Once you know your billing cycle, check the current winter-averaging dates and review your irrigation schedule. Leaks and unnecessary outdoor watering during that period can affect the calculation. The previous owner’s sewer charge is useful background, but your account’s billing basis still needs confirmation.

links.label: SAWS residential water and sewer rates

blocks.text: Build the budget around the correct rate year

Ask the seller for recent bills they are comfortable sharing, with account details removed. Compare usage as well as the total. Your household size, watering habits and move-in timing may differ from theirs.

There is a timely reason to check the effective date: in an October 9, 2026 announcement, SAWS said City Council had approved a rate adjustment beginning January 1, 2027. If you are buying this fall, ask for a budget estimate that accounts for the change. An average increase in a news announcement is not a quote for your home.

links.label: SAWS rate approval announcement dated October 9

blocks.text: Learn to read your meter after moving in

After moving in, learn to read the meter you actually have. SAWS explains that its electronic meter’s flow-rate screen should read zero when water is not being used. Its leak-check instructions call for turning off inside and outside faucets and comparing meter readings. Allow for appliances or equipment that may still be using water, and get professional help if the result is unclear. Do not treat a quick meter check as a substitute for an inspection.
Keep these answers together before moving

items: Water provider and wastewater billing provider confirmed for the exact address
Individual or shared service arrangement understood
Start date confirmed and coordinated with possession of the home
Deposit, applicable fees and first-bill expectations recorded
Initial sewer billing basis and winter-averaging schedule checked
Current and upcoming rates included in the household budget

blocks.text: Frequently asked questions
Does SAWS provide both services everywhere it serves? Its water and sewer service areas differ. Confirm each service and billing provider for the property. See the service-area maps linked above.
Where do I transfer an existing SAWS account? Use the Stop or Transfer Service route through My Account. Confirm the dates with SAWS before the move.
Will my sewer bill match the seller’s? Do not assume it will. Ask how SAWS will calculate your new account’s sewer usage until an applicable average is available.
General homebuyer education. Confirm service eligibility, account requirements and charges with the responsible utility for the specific property.

title: San Antonio HOA Documents: What Buyers Should Review
description: Organize HOA restrictions, resale certificates, assessments, contacts and contractual deadlines before your purchase.

blocks.text: Buying a San Antonio home with a homeowners association? Ask for the current restrictions, bylaws, rules and resale certificate early. Then review the costs, property-specific issues and deadlines with your real-estate team. An HOA’s pool photos or a listing’s dues figure can be a useful starting point, but you still need the documents that apply to the home you are buying.
Here is a practical way to organize that review before your purchase moves further along.
1. Ask for the complete packet

TREC’s HOA addendum calls the restrictions, bylaws, rules and resale certificate “Subdivision Information.” The resale certificate summarizes association and property information. Read it alongside the governing documents so you can connect the financial details with the rules you would live under.

Confirm that the association name and property address match your purchase. Ask whether another association also applies to the lot, and check that every referenced attachment arrived. Save the original files and the delivery email together.

This guide focuses on homes subject to mandatory property-owners-association membership. TREC’s HOA addendum is not for condominiums; confirm the correct contract and documents for your ownership type.

links.label: Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association

blocks.text: 2. Read the financial details together

TREC’s resale-certificate form includes regular assessments and their frequency, special assessments, unpaid property balances, approved capital expenditures, reserves, judgments, pending lawsuits and transfer-related fees. It also calls for attachments including the current operating budget and balance sheet.
Use those records to build a short question list:

items: What recurring amount should I budget, and when is it due?
Are there special assessments or unpaid amounts connected to this property?
What major projects are approved, and what money is available for them?
Which closing charges will each party pay under the signed agreement?

blocks.text: Ask for explanations of unfamiliar entries. A dollar amount makes more sense when you understand what it covers and when payment is expected.

links.label: TREC Form 37-5: Subdivision Information, Including Resale Certificate

blocks.text: 3. Match the rules to your plans
Write down how you expect to use the property. You might want a fence, a storage shed, a different exterior paint color, space for an RV or the flexibility to rent the home later.

Locate the relevant rules and ask the association’s authorized contact about the approval process. Request written clarification when the language is unclear. Avoid assuming that a neighboring property proves your proposed change is permitted.

The resale certificate also addresses known restriction violations and governmental notices. If an issue is listed, ask your agent and title team how it will be addressed in this transaction. Get legal advice when the answer involves interpreting your rights.

links.label: TREC Form 37-5: Subdivision Information, Including Resale Certificate

blocks.text: 4. Calendar the HOA deadlines when you sign
TREC lists Form 36-11 as effective July 1, 2026. Its document-delivery choices have different consequences, so ask your agent to explain the box selected in your agreement before signing.

One detail deserves attention: under Paragraph A(2), where the buyer obtains the information, receipt is deemed to occur on the actual receipt date or the date specified in that paragraph, whichever is earlier. Waiting for the documents to appear in your inbox can therefore be risky.
Have your agent or attorney identify the applicable dates and notice requirements from your signed contract. Keep these in a shared checklist rather than relying on a general online deadline.

links.label: Addendum for Property Subject to Mandatory Membership in a Property Owners Association

blocks.text: 5. Find the association’s contact information

Texas provides a public HOA management-certificate database at hoa.texas.gov. Search by association name or location to help identify the managing contact. A management certificate serves a different purpose from the resale certificate for your purchase; keep track of both.
If you cannot locate a management certificate, TREC suggests checking with the local county clerk or the HOA. TREC maintains the database but does not regulate HOA activities.

links.label: Why TREC Maintains an HOA Management Certificate Database
HOA Management Certificate Website Now Live

blocks.text: Bring these questions to your next conversation

Before your next call, gather the property address, association name, complete packet, signed addendum and questions about costs or intended improvements. Mark anything missing and who is following up. A clear document checklist gives you and your real-estate team a more useful conversation about the home.
For help organizing your San Antonio home search, contact Emily Russell.
General educational information. This article is not legal advice. Confirm property-specific obligations and contractual rights with the appropriate professionals.
